newsitem.title: USA: U.S. nickel sees no quick boost from Inco dispute.
newsitem.headline: U.S. nickel sees no quick boost from Inco dispute.

text.p: The lackluster nickel market, battered further by last week's low-priced U.S. Mint tender, barely raised an eyebrow at Inco's shutdown of its Manitoba plant, although the market could be affected if the dispute drags out, traders and analysts cautioned.
"Psychologically, it could move the market within a couple of weeks," said analyst Chuck Bradford of UBS Securities. "But it would need to take a month to have a real effect."
Manitoba produces 100 million pounds of nickel a year, 20 percent on Inco's output. In addition, last week a furnace blast shut a third of production at Inco's Indonesian plant.

Inco decided to shut down the Thompson plant in Manitoba after the union said 71 percent of workers rejected the company's labor deal. The union offered to continue working, United Steelworkers of American official Bob Desjarlais said.

Although traders noted that Thompson produced much of Inco's refined nickel destined for the U.S. market, "if you look back at history, Inco has always prepared for such eventualities," a Canadian nickel source said.
Inco said earlier Monday that supplies to customers will not be disrupted - but a company spokesman declined to say for how long deliveries could be maintained.
Traders said nickel in the U.S. was plentiful, with stainless steel producers trying to slim down their finished steel inventories.
"The stainless steel makers are not in the market to look for nickel right now. There is so much scrap and ferro-nickel around," a New York trader said.

The extent of the lackluster spot market was highlighted by last week's U.S. Mint tender for Western quality nickel which was won by a trader at premiums of about five cents per pound over LME cash, including delivery and 30-days financing.
"I don't know how they can possibly make any money on that unless they took a position when the market was low," a U.S. nickel merchant said.

Furthermore, the U.S. government stockpile failed to sell any nickel in its sale offer last week. "Traders are stuffed to the gills with nickel. We have been offered tonnes of it from Europe at good discounts," the New York trader said.
Consequently premiums have weakened to 5 to 10 cents per pound over LME cash, down from 6 to 12 cents last month.
The stainless mills are said to be buying nickel cathode hand-to-mouth.
The mills are still bruised from their climbdown earlier this year - planned stainless price hikes had to be ditched because European prices were so weak.

Bradford said U.S. stainless prices were about $2,200 a tonne with inventories six to seven percent too high at well over three months, while European stainless prices have edged up to $1,850. A five percent European price hike for deliveries from October was largely successful and a similar hike in November was also due.

"There is also talk of another five percent increase in January but that has not been announced. Once they go beyond the November rise, it means the U.S. can also go for something," Bradford said. "We probably need a European price of $2,000 a tonne to get a U.S. price increase."
